questions.text: Thinking through someone's difficulties rarely makes me care about them more.
I think it is important to make a stand and defend it.
I sense when a group has collectively decided on something before any formal vote or discussion.
I often forgo recognition so that others can be acknowledged instead.
I can be in the midst of uncertainty and still feel fundamentally okay.
I routinely upgrade my skills specifically to increase my market value.
I detect when a group's energy shifts from casual to serious.
I tend to miss it when someone laughs at the wrong moment because they are uncomfortable.
I commit to a decision and adjust quickly if the outcome isn't what I expected.
I frequently volunteer to be the spokesperson or point person.
Each new encounter with suffering still matters to me; it doesn't become routine.
I feel that my creative projects deserve the same level of investment I would give to a professional obligation.
I tend to miss when someone includes me in a plan out of obligation rather than desire.
When someone trusts me with their pain, I want to hold it with care.
I routinely go out of my way to introduce people to opportunities they deserve.
I routinely proofread, edit, or review other people's work without being asked.
I register the weight of another person's pain not just intellectually but as something that genuinely matters to me and moves me.
I make it a point to arrive early to appointments and meetings.
Suffering among people whose lives are very different from mine carries little weight for me.
I tend to view my savings as a tool for my own future, not a resource for others.
A tense silence in a conversation produces a physical knot in my stomach almost instantly.
I feel comfortable contributing to something that bears the group's stamp, not mine.
I tend not to read meaning into someone choosing to communicate by text versus calling versus meeting in person.
I would rather let the team take extra time than force a call that divides people.
I track the time I spend on different activities to understand where my hours go.
I experience the onset of emotion as a sudden physical sensation before I can even name what I'm feeling.
I think it is important to remain open and willing to shift with the group.
I experience change as something to be navigated calmly rather than something that triggers alarm.
I notice that even reading a particularly moving paragraph in a book can make my throat tighten.
I notice when a conversation partner's pupils dilate or contract in response to what is being discussed.
I get bored when a process becomes too routine and look for ways to shake things up.
I prepare for meetings by reviewing agendas and relevant materials in advance.
I notice that waiting for important outcomes produces alertness in me, not agitation.
I am drawn to moments where one person's decision changes everything.
Someone's serious suffering leaves me with little concern for what happens to them.
I feel more in control when I'm free to react to what's actually happening rather than following a script.
